p: As in 11:1, "brothers" means fellow believers, men and women. New here: Jewish believers use it of uncircumcised Gentiles.
b: For the word itself, adelphoi, and why the Plain English Translation keeps "brothers" for a mixed group, see the note on 11:1. What this chapter adds is who is being called "brother." The Judean teachers treat the Gentile believers at Antioch as brothers who still lack circumcision, and the council's letter goes further: the apostles and elders, "who are brothers," write "to the brothers of Gentile birth" (15:23). Jews had used the word for fellow Jews (2:29; 13:26); here it crosses the line of circumcision before the question of circumcision is even settled.

t: Must a Gentile become a Jew?
p: Jews of the time disagreed about whether Gentiles who honored God had to be circumcised.
b: The teachers from Judea were not inventing a strange rule. A man who wanted to join Israel became a convert by circumcision (Genesis 17:12–14; Exodus 12:48). But Jews disagreed about Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God without converting. Josephus tells how King Izates of Adiabene was told by one Jewish teacher that he could worship God without circumcision, and then by another, Eleazar from Galilee, that he was breaking the law by staying uncircumcised; he was circumcised (Antiquities 20.34–48). Later rabbis taught that righteous Gentiles have a share in the world to come without becoming Jews. What was new at Antioch was the question in a messianic setting: were believing Gentiles part of God's people as Gentiles? Paula Fredriksen argues that most of the first apostles assumed they were, because the prophets pictured the nations turning to Israel's God as nations, not converts (Isaiah 2:2–4; Zechariah 8:20–23).
r: Genesis 17:12–14; Exodus 12:48; Isaiah 2:2–4; Zechariah 8:20–23; Galatians 2:3–5; Galatians 5:2–6

t: Acts 15 and Galatians 2: the same meeting?
p: Paul tells of a Jerusalem meeting in Galatians 2. Scholars disagree on which visit in Acts it matches.
b: Paul's own account (Galatians 2:1–10) tells of a private meeting with James, Cephas and John, who shook hands with him and Barnabas as partners and asked only that they remember the poor. The same meeting: most critical scholars (Haenchen, Fitzmyer, Pervo) and many others since J. B. Lightfoot equate it with Acts 15, and explain the differences (no decree in Galatians) as Paul's and Luke's different interests. The famine visit: Ramsay, F. F. Bruce, Richard Longenecker and Ben Witherington match Galatians 2 with the visit of 11:29–30, so Galatians was written before this council, which would explain why Paul never cites its decree there. A blend: some think Luke combined two meetings, one about circumcision and one about food, into one scene. Each view has to explain why Paul says Titus was not forced to be circumcised (Galatians 2:3) and why Paul's letters never mention the decree.

p: The delegation walked about 300 miles, through the coast towns and Samaria, sharing the news as they went.
b: From Antioch to Jerusalem by land was roughly three hundred miles, two weeks or more on foot. The road ran down the Phoenician coast, through Tyre and Sidon, where churches had been planted by believers scattered after Stephen's death (11:19), and then through Samaria, where Philip had preached (8:5–25). Luke notes that these churches, made up of Hellenist Jews and Samaritans, were glad to hear of Gentiles turning to God. The opposition came from Judea, not from them.

p: The Greek hairesis meant a party or school of thought. It later gave English the word "heresy."
b: Luke uses hairesis for the Sadducees (5:17), the Pharisees (here and 26:5) and the followers of Jesus themselves (24:5, 14; 28:22). This site renders it "party" for the Jewish groups and "sect" where outsiders use it of the Way, so the reader can follow the one Greek word. Josephus uses it for the Jewish "schools" of Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes. It was not yet an insult; only later Christian writers used it for false teaching. That believers could still be called Pharisees shows that joining the Jesus movement did not mean leaving one's Jewish party. Paul himself still says, "I am a Pharisee" (23:6; compare Philippians 3:5). These believing Pharisees argued from the Torah, and their position was the more obvious reading of Genesis 17.

a: through my mouth that the Gentiles were to hear
p: Peter points back to Acts 10–11, where the Spirit came on Cornelius' household before anyone was baptized.
b: "From the first days" may sound like a long time, but the Cornelius episode was perhaps ten years earlier. Peter's speech, his last in Acts, sums up 10:1–11:18 in three steps: God chose Peter to preach to Gentiles; God gave them the Spirit "as he had given him to us" (compare 10:44–47; 11:15–17); and God cleansed their hearts, recalling the vision's words, "What God has made clean, you must not call common" (10:15). The argument is from experience read as God's verdict: what God has already done, the church must not undo. After this Peter disappears from the story of Acts.

p: A rare title: Acts uses it twice, here and in the prayer before Matthias was chosen.
b: Kardiognōstēs appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Acts: in the prayer when the apostles cast lots (1:24) and here. The idea is old: "the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7), and Jeremiah's God searches the heart (Jeremiah 17:10). Peter's point is that circumcision is a mark on the body, but God, who sees inside, had already accepted these Gentiles. Paul argues in the same way that true circumcision is a matter of the heart (Romans 2:29).

a: by faith he made their hearts clean
p: Peter uses the language of purity: God has "cleaned" the Gentiles, so they are no longer unclean to Jews.
b: The verb is katharizō, the word of Peter's vision: "What God has made clean, you must not call common" (10:15; 11:9). Many Jews of the time treated Gentiles as a source of impurity to be kept at a distance, especially at meals (10:28; 11:3). Peter now says that God has done the cleansing, not by washing or circumcision but "by faith." Fredriksen and others point out that this is purity language, not a rejection of the Torah for Jews: the issue is whether Gentiles are fit company for God's people. Compare Psalm 51:10, the prayer for a clean heart, and Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God cleans his people and gives them his Spirit.

p: In Jewish teaching the Torah was a welcome yoke. Peter's words are a hard saying, and readers take them differently.
b: Jews spoke gladly of "taking on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven" by reciting the Shema, and "the yoke of the commandments" (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). The Mishnah says that whoever takes on the yoke of Torah is freed from other yokes (Avot 3:5). So Peter's line, a yoke "neither our ancestors nor we ourselves had the strength to carry," is striking from a Jewish apostle. A complaint about the law: many Christian readers take it as a judgment that the law could not be kept perfectly (compare Galatians 3:10). A word about Gentiles: others note that the issue is laying the whole Torah on Gentiles as a condition of salvation; Jews like Peter went on keeping it. Jewish readers have pointed out that the picture of the law as a crushing burden is a caricature of how Jews experienced it. Jesus offered his own yoke, "kind to wear" (Matthew 11:30).

p: Peter reverses the expected order: not Gentiles saved as Jews are, but Jews saved as Gentiles are.
b: One would expect a Jewish apostle to say that Gentiles are saved the same way Jews are. Peter says the opposite: "we" are saved the same way "they" are, by grace. The sentence is often read in light of Paul's teaching that a person is justified by faith, not works of the law (Galatians 2:16), and Protestant readers have seen in it the heart of the gospel. Catholic and Orthodox readers agree that salvation is by grace, while reading grace as also working through baptism and a life of faith. Philipp Vielhauer pointed out an oddity: the only Pauline-sounding statement about the law in Acts is put in Peter's mouth, and its reason, that the law is a yoke no one could bear (15:10), is not Paul's own argument, for Paul calls himself blameless under the law (Philippians 3:6). Others answer that Galatians 2:15–16 shows Peter and Paul shared the conviction that Jews too are saved by grace.

p: In Jerusalem Luke puts Barnabas first again, as in the early chapters. He was the one Jerusalem knew and trusted.
b: From 13:13 on, Luke usually writes "Paul and Barnabas." Here and in the letter (15:25) the order turns back to "Barnabas and Paul." Barnabas had been a trusted member of the Jerusalem church from the start (4:36–37), had vouched for Saul when others feared him (9:27), and had been sent by Jerusalem to Antioch (11:22). In Jerusalem's eyes he was the senior partner. The report takes the form of "signs and wonders," the phrase used for the works of Moses and of the apostles (7:36; 2:43; 5:12): God's deeds proved God's will.

p: James the brother of Jesus (see 12:17), now speaking last and giving the ruling.
b: For who this James is, see the note on 12:17. What is new here is his role. Peter has spoken and Barnabas and Paul have told their story, and James speaks last and sums up: the place of the one who presides. Later tradition called him "James the Just" for his devotion to the law, and that is what gives the ruling its weight. The leader most loyal to the Torah is the one who rules that Gentile believers need not keep it, and he does it by an argument from the Torah's own prophets and from its laws for foreigners (15:16–21). He appears again in 21:18–25, where the decree is recalled and Paul is asked to show his own loyalty to the law.

p: James calls Peter by the old Hebrew form of his name, which appears only here and in 2 Peter 1:1.
b: Elsewhere Peter is "Simon" (a Greek name close in sound) or "Peter" (Greek for the Aramaic Kepha, rock). Symeōn is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew Shimon, the patriarch's name (Genesis 29:33). Only James here and 2 Peter 1:1 use it for Peter. Many commentators take it as a true-to-life touch: James, the Jerusalem leader, speaks of his colleague in the Jerusalem way.

p: In the Greek Bible laos, "people," is the regular word for Israel. James uses it for Gentiles.
b: In the Septuagint, laos means God's own people, Israel, while the other peoples are ethnē, "the nations." James joins the two in a startling phrase: God has taken "from the nations a people." Nils Dahl showed how close it is to Zechariah 2:11 in the Greek, "many nations will flee to the Lord ... and they will become a people to him." The point is not that the church replaces Israel: James goes on to say that David's house will be rebuilt first (15:16). It is that the nations now join Israel's God without ceasing to be nations. Readers who hold different views of the church and Israel read the verse in their own way (see the topic page).
orig: λαὸν τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ (laon tō onomati autou)

p: Amos promised that David's ruined house would stand again. Jews at Qumran also read it as a promise for the last days.
b: Skēnē is a tent or booth; Amos' Hebrew is sukkah, a shelter of branches. A tent that has fallen is a picture of David's dynasty in ruins after the exile. Readings: the Messiah's kingdom: most interpreters take James to mean that God has raised up David's heir, Jesus, and with him a restored Israel (compare 2:30–36; 13:22–23, 34). The end-time temple: Richard Bauckham argues that Jews read the "tent of David" as the temple of the last days, which the church now is. The Dead Sea Scrolls also quote the verse: the Florilegium (4Q174) applies it to the "branch of David" who will arise in the last days, and the Damascus Document (7:16) to the books of the law. The opening "After these things I will come back" is not Amos' wording but resembles Jeremiah 12:15 in the Greek.

a: so that those who are left of humankind may seek out the Lord
t: James quotes the Greek of Amos
p: The Hebrew of Amos 9:12 says Israel will possess "what is left of Edom." The Greek says the rest of humankind will seek the Lord.
b: Amos' Hebrew says that David's restored house will take possession of what is left of Edom and of all the nations over whom the LORD's name has been called. The Septuagint reads "so that the rest of humankind may seek out" (adding "the Lord" in some copies). Two small differences in Hebrew letters explain it: yireshu "possess" read as yidreshu "seek," and Edom read as adam "humankind." Questions follow. Did James argue from the Greek? A Jerusalem leader speaking to Jews would more likely quote Hebrew, so many critics think Luke composed the speech from his Greek Bible. Or a Hebrew text like it? Others note that the Hebrew already ends with "all the nations over whom my name has been called," which already makes James' point, and that a Hebrew text with "seek" may have existed. Either way, the nations belong to the Lord as nations.
orig: ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων (ekzētēsōsin hoi kataloipoi tōn anthrōpōn)

a: over whom my name has been called
p: A Hebrew way of saying "who belong to me." A name called over a city, a house or a people marks the owner.
b: To have someone's name "called over" you means you belong to him. Moses promises Israel, "Every people on earth will see that the LORD's name has been called over you" (Deuteronomy 28:10). A conqueror's name was called over a captured city (2 Samuel 12:28). Amos' line says that some of the nations will belong to the LORD too. For James, that settles the question: the prophet speaks of the nations belonging to God as nations, not of nations who first become Israelites. The perfect tense in the Greek, "has been called," fits his claim that it has already happened.
orig: ἐφ’ οὓς ἐπικέκληται τὸ ὄνομά μου (eph’ hous epikeklētai to onoma mou)

p: James ends the quotation with words not from Amos but close to Isaiah 45:21.
b: Amos 9:12 ends, "says the LORD, who is doing this." James adds "known from ages past," which seems to come from Isaiah 45:21, where the LORD asks the nations, "Who announced this long ago?" (Isaiah 45:21). The next verse goes on: "Turn to me, all you ends of the earth, and be saved" (Isaiah 45:22). James' point: welcoming the nations is not a new idea forced on the church by events, but God's plan announced long before. The words can also be punctuated "the Lord, who makes these things known from long ago" (see the variant).

p: James says "I judge." Readers ask whether he was giving his opinion or ruling as the council's head.
b: The Greek egō krinō can mean "I think" or "I rule." James as presiding bishop: early tradition, as reported by Eusebius, made James the first bishop of Jerusalem, and many readers, ancient and modern, see him here giving the deciding word. Peter's primacy: Catholic interpreters often stress that Peter spoke first and settled the principle, and James applied it. A shared decision: Luke says the apostles and elders decided "together with the whole church" (15:22), and Presbyterian and Congregational readers point to this as a pattern for church decisions. Luke's own interest is that everyone agreed and the Spirit led (15:25, 28). See the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter.

t: What were the four rules for?
p: The four items match the laws for foreigners living in Israel in Leviticus 17–18. Other readings exist.
b: The laws for the resident foreigner: the most widely held view links the list to Leviticus 17–18, the laws that bind "any foreigner living among them": sacrifices to other gods (Leviticus 17:7–9), eating blood (Leviticus 17:10–12), meat not drained of blood (Leviticus 17:13–15) and forbidden sexual unions (Leviticus 18:6–26). In 15:29 the order is exactly that of Leviticus. Gentile believers were to live like the foreigners among Israel, who were not circumcised but were kept from what made the land unclean. Rules for shared meals: others stress the practical goal of letting Jewish and Gentile believers eat together. Moral rules: the Western text turns them into a ban on idolatry, sexual sin and murder (see the variant). The laws of Noah: later rabbis taught seven commandments binding on all descendants of Noah (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 56a–b), an interesting parallel, but written down later.

p: Meat from animals killed without draining their blood, such as game caught in snares.
b: Pniktos means "choked, strangled." An animal killed that way keeps its blood in the meat. Leviticus 17:13 requires a hunter, Israelite or foreigner, to "pour out its blood and cover it with dirt." The Jewish philosopher Philo condemns people who strangle animals to keep the blood in the flesh as a delicacy (On the Special Laws 4.122). So this rule is a special case of the ban on blood, which is why some early copies left it out when the list was read as moral rules (see the variant).

p: The word covers every kind of sexual sin. Here it may point especially to the forbidden marriages of Leviticus 18.
b: Porneia is broad: prostitution, adultery, any sex outside marriage. Set in a list that follows Leviticus 17–18, many scholars think it means above all the unions Leviticus 18 forbids to Israelites and foreigners alike, such as marriage to close relatives, which Greek and Roman law sometimes allowed. Others take it in its broad sense, because pagan cults and festivals often included sexual license. The same pair, food offered to idols and porneia, appears in the letters to Pergamum and Thyatira: "eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual sin" (Revelation 2:14).

p: James' last sentence is puzzling. Interpreters offer at least three explanations.
b: Respect for Jewish neighbors: since Moses is read every Sabbath in every city, Jews everywhere know these laws, and Gentile believers should not offend them. The rules are not new: the four items come from Moses himself, as everyone who hears the Torah read knows; Gentiles are asked only what Moses already asked of foreigners. Moses is in no danger: Jews will go on keeping the law, so freeing Gentiles from circumcision takes nothing from Israel. The verse also gives a glimpse of the synagogue as Paul found it: the Torah read aloud each Sabbath in Greek-speaking cities, with Gentiles in the audience (13:15, 27, 42–44).

p: Paul's next partner. His letters call him Silvanus, and he later helped Peter write.
b: Silas is probably a Greek form of the Aramaic name Saul; Silvanus, the name in the letters, is its Latin form. He was a leader and a prophet in Jerusalem (15:32) and, like Paul, a Roman citizen (16:37). He became Paul's partner on the second journey and is named as co-sender of 1 and 2 Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Paul recalls that he preached at Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:19). 1 Peter 5:12 says the letter was written through Silvanus, which may mean he carried it or helped compose it.

p: It names only Antioch and the province of Syria and Cilicia, where the dispute started. Paul's newer churches are not named.
b: Syria and Cilicia were governed together as one Roman province at this time, and Antioch was its capital. The letter answers the trouble that began there (15:1). Yet in 16:4 Paul delivers the decrees to the towns of Lycaonia and Galatia as well. Some scholars see this as Luke widening the decree to all Gentile churches; others think it is natural for a ruling to travel beyond its first addressees. The letter's opening, "greetings" (chairein), is the standard Greek letter form, found in the New Testament only here, in the letter of Claudius Lysias (23:26), and in the letter of James (James 1:1), whose author tradition names as the same James.

a: For the Holy Spirit has decided, and so have we
t: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"
p: The council uses the formula of a Greek city decree, with the Holy Spirit named first.
b: Greek cities published their laws under the heading "It seemed good (edoxe) to the council and to the people." The same verb runs through this chapter (15:22, 25, 28). By naming the Holy Spirit first, the letter claims that the decision was God's, reached through the gathered church. Later church councils echoed the formula, and it became a key text for how churches understand councils and church authority (see the "Where Christians differ" card). The decree is called "necessary things," not a new law of salvation: nothing heavier than these is laid on Gentile believers.
orig: ἔδοξεν γὰρ τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ καὶ ἡμῖν (edoxen gar tō pneumati tō hagiō kai hēmin)

p: Paul never cites the decree in his letters, yet the churches kept its food rules for centuries.
b: Eidōlothyta, meat from animals sacrificed in temples, was the meat on sale in the market and served at feasts. Paul's letters deal with it at length (1 Corinthians 8–10; Romans 14) without mentioning a Jerusalem decree: he allows eating market meat with a clear conscience but forbids taking part in temple meals. Revelation condemns those who teach believers to "eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual sin" (Revelation 2:14). The Didache (6:3) urges strict avoidance of idol food, and the martyrs of Lyons in AD 177 protested that Christians would not even eat the blood of animals (reported by Eusebius, Church History 5.1.26). Tertullian also says Christians did not eat blood (Apology 9). Whether the rule on blood still binds, even for medicine, is set out tradition by tradition in the "Where Christians differ" card on Leviticus 17. Acts adds two things to that debate. Here the rule is one of four "necessary things" laid on Gentile believers for a shared life, not a condition of salvation (15:28). And Calvin, on 15:20, held that the decree was a rule of love for its time, to spare Jewish believers offense, with only the ban on sexual sin binding for good; Jehovah's Witnesses, by contrast, read "keep away from blood" here as a lasting command (see the Leviticus card).
r: 1 Corinthians 8:1–13; 1 Corinthians 10:14–33; Romans 14:1–23; Revelation 2:14; Revelation 2:20; 21:25; Leviticus 17:10–14

p: Acts names several Christian prophets. Their work here is to encourage, the same word as the letter's "comfort."
b: Agabus and others came from Jerusalem to Antioch as prophets (11:27–28), Antioch had prophets and teachers (13:1), and Philip's four daughters prophesied (21:9). Judas and Silas use their gift to "urge on" (parakaleō) the brothers, the verb behind the "comfort" (paraklēsis) that the letter brought (15:31). Paul later writes that prophecy builds up, encourages and comforts (1 Corinthians 14:3). New Testament prophecy was not only prediction.

t: John Mark, the cause of the split
p: The young man who turned back at Perga (13:13). Paul refuses him; Barnabas takes him. Later the breach healed.
b: For Mark's family and his first journey, see the notes on 12:12, 13:5 and 13:13. New here is the quarrel. Barnabas wanted to give his cousin (Colossians 4:10) a second chance; Paul judged that a man who had walked away once should not come on a hard journey. Luke names no winner: Barnabas and Mark go to Cyprus, Paul and Silas overland, and the church gains two missions. Paul's letters show the breach healed: Mark is with Paul later (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24), and Paul asks for him because he is useful in the ministry (2 Timothy 4:11).

p: Luke does not hide that two leaders of the church fell out. His word gives English "paroxysm."
b: Paroxysmos is a sharp provocation, an angry flare-up. The verb from the same root describes Paul's spirit in Athens, "stirred to anger" by idols (17:16), and Hebrews uses the noun in a good sense, for stirring one another up to love (Hebrews 10:24). Luke tells only that the quarrel was about Mark. Paul's letter to the Galatians adds that at Antioch even Barnabas was carried along when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles (Galatians 2:13), and some scholars think that incident lay behind the split. Chrysostom commented that the quarrel had good results, since two missions went out instead of one.

a: His mother was a Jewish believer, and his father a Greek.
p: Later Jewish law counts the child of a Jewish mother as Jewish. Whether that rule held in Paul's day is debated.
b: Timothy had a Jewish mother (named Eunice in 2 Timothy 1:5, with his grandmother Lois) and a Greek father. Jewish by his mother: the rabbinic rule that Jewish identity passes through the mother is found in the Mishnah (Kiddushin 3:12), and many commentators (Bruce among them) assume it, so Paul was regularizing the status of a Jew who had never been circumcised. Not yet a rule: Shaye Cohen has argued that the matrilineal principle is not attested before the Mishnah and that in the first century a son of a Gentile father would usually be counted a Gentile; on this view Paul's act needs another explanation. Somewhere between: others think local Jews would have seen him as a Jew who had failed to be circumcised, which is why Luke says "since everyone knew his father was Greek" (16:3).

p: Right after the council freed Gentiles from circumcision, Paul circumcises Timothy. Paul's letters seem to say he would not.
b: Paul writes that Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised (Galatians 2:3), and warns Gentile believers that if they accept circumcision Christ will be of no benefit to them (Galatians 5:2). Consistent: most traditional and many modern readers (Bruce, Witherington) answer that the council's question was whether Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised not for salvation but so that Jews would accept him, as Paul says he became "as a Jew" to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). Luke's portrait: critical scholars such as Haenchen and Pervo think the story fits Luke's picture of a law-keeping Paul (21:21–26) better than the Paul of Galatians and doubt it happened. Paul the Jew: scholars of the "Paul within Judaism" school (Fredriksen, Nanos) see no conflict: Paul never told Jews to stop circumcising their sons (compare 21:21).

p: The Greek dogmata names the council's rulings here and "Caesar's decrees" in 17:7. Luke sets the two side by side.
b: Dogma meant an official decree: Caesar Augustus' census decree (Luke 2:1), the emperor's rulings (17:7). Luke uses it for the Jerusalem rulings too, and only a few verses later Paul is accused of acting against "Caesar's decrees." The pairing suggests Luke's theme: the church lives under the rulings of the apostles and the Spirit, and the world's rulers sometimes see that as a rival authority. English "dogma," a church teaching, comes from this word through the later church.

a: day after day their numbers swelled
p: Luke marks each stage of Acts with a short report of growth. This one closes the story of the council.
b: Acts is built in panels, each closed by a summary: the word of God grew (6:7), the church had peace and grew (9:31), the word grew and multiplied (12:24), here the churches grew stronger and more numerous, and the word grew mightily (19:20), until Paul preaches openly in Rome (28:31). Many scholars treat these as Luke's chapter breaks. This one shows the decree did its work: the Gentile churches were strengthened, not divided.

p: The phrase decides where the "Galatians" of Paul's letter lived. Scholars split between north and south.
b: South Galatia: the Roman province of Galatia included the towns of the first journey, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (13–14). William Ramsay argued that "the Phrygian and Galatian country" means the Phrygian district inside the province, so Paul's letter to the Galatians went to those churches (the view of Bruce, Hemer and many others). North Galatia: the old view, still held by many scholars (Lightfoot, Betz, Martyn), is that Paul now went into ethnic Galatia, the Celtic lands around Ancyra (modern Ankara), and founded the churches of the letter on this trip (compare 18:23; Galatians 4:13). The grammar matters too. In the critical text "they crossed" is the main verb and "having been kept from" (kōlythentes) is a participle placed after it; such a participle often describes something that happened first, so they may have been barred from Asia before they went through this country, which would send them north or northwest. The Byzantine text and the KJV make the crossing a participle too ("when they had gone throughout," see the variant), which loosens the order further. The Plain English Translation joins the two with "and" so as not to settle the question.

t: How did the Spirit stop them?
p: Luke does not say. Readers have suggested a prophet's word, a dream, an illness, or closed roads.
b: Twice in two verses the way is blocked, first by "the Holy Spirit," then by "the Spirit of Jesus" (16:7), before a vision opens the way to Macedonia (16:9). Luke does not say how the Spirit spoke. Elsewhere it is through prophets (13:1–2; 21:11), and some suggest that here too. Others connect it with the illness Paul mentions in Galatians 4:13. Luke's point is that the mission went where God sent it: the province of Asia, with Ephesus, would come later (19:1–10). Calling the Spirit "the Spirit of Jesus" puts the risen Jesus in the place of the God of Israel, who guides his people by his Spirit.

p: Alexandria Troas, a Roman colony and harbor near ancient Troy, the crossing point to Europe.
b: Troas was the port where travelers took ship from Asia to Macedonia. It lay about fifteen miles south of the ruins of Troy, the city of Homer's Iliad. Augustus made it a Roman colony. Paul came back to Troas later and found "an open door" (2 Corinthians 2:12), and it is there that Eutychus fell from a window during a long sermon (20:5–12).

p: Who was he? Readers have guessed Luke himself, the angel of the nation (Origen), or simply a figure in a dream.
b: Visions guide Paul at turning points in Acts (9:12; 18:9–10; 22:17–21; 23:11; 27:23–24). How did Paul know the man was Macedonian? Perhaps by his dress or speech, or because he named his country. William Ramsay suggested that the man was Luke himself, whom Paul had met at Troas, since the "we" begins in the next verse; this is a guess most scholars find attractive but unprovable. Origen took him as the guardian angel of Macedonia, on the model of the angels of nations in Daniel 10:20–21 (Homilies on Luke 12). Readers of Greek history may also have thought of a Macedonian, Alexander the Great, crossing the other way, from Europe into Asia.

p: Here the narrator suddenly says "we." The "we" sections are one of the great puzzles of Acts.
b: From 16:10 to 16:17 the story is told in the first person plural; "we" returns at 20:5–21:18 and 27:1–28:16. An eyewitness: the traditional view, held by Irenaeus and by many modern scholars (Fitzmyer, Hemer, Keener), is that the author joined Paul at Troas and later rejoined him at Philippi (20:5–6). A travel diary: others think the author used a companion's notes, keeping the "we." A literary device: Vernon Robbins argued that ancient sea-voyage stories were often told in the first person; critics replied that many voyages are told in the third person. A claim to be there: Richard Pervo and others see the "we" as the author's way of claiming authority for his story. The Western text has an earlier "we" at Antioch (11:28).

p: With a following wind the trip took two days. The reverse journey later took five (20:6).
b: From Troas the ship ran northwest to the island of Samothrace, with its high mountain and its famous shrine of the Great Gods, anchored there for the night, and reached Neapolis (modern Kavala), the port of Philippi, the next day. Luke's word euthydromeō is a sailor's term: to run before the wind on a straight course. When Paul made the same crossing the other way, it took five days (20:6). Luke's precise travel notes are one reason many historians think the "we" passages rest on firsthand memory.

p: Philippi was settled with Roman army veterans and governed like a small copy of Rome.
b: Philip II of Macedon, Alexander's father, gave the city its name. In 42 BC Antony and Octavian defeated Caesar's assassins Brutus and Cassius on the plain outside it, and veterans were settled there; after 31 BC Octavian (soon Augustus) refounded it as a Roman colony. Its citizens were Roman citizens, its official language was Latin, and two magistrates with rod-bearers ruled it like little consuls. That background explains the charges in 16:21 ("we, as Romans") and Paul's appeal to citizenship (16:37). When Paul later tells the Philippians that their citizenship (politeuma) is in heaven (Philippians 3:20), he is speaking to people proud of being citizens of Rome far from Rome.

t: A "place of prayer" by the river
p: The Greek proseuchē was a common name for a synagogue, especially among Jews of the Greek world.
b: Proseuchē means "prayer," and also a house of prayer: inscriptions from Egypt use it for synagogues, and so do Philo (Against Flaccus 41–53) and Josephus, who mentions a large proseuchē at Tiberias (Life 277). At Philippi it may have been a building or an open-air spot near the water, useful for washing. The Gangites river (or a smaller stream near the gate) runs west of the city. Only women are mentioned. Later Jewish law required ten men for some prayers in public worship (Mishnah Megillah 4:3), so some think the Jewish community there was very small; but women gathering for prayer needed no such quorum.

p: Purple cloth was costly. Inscriptions from Thyatira mention its dyers, and Lydia was probably well off.
b: Thyatira, in the region of Lydia in Asia Minor, was known for its trade guilds, among them dyers, attested in Greek inscriptions. Purple dye came either from murex shellfish, very expensive, or from the madder root, used in that region. A seller of purple worked with the clothing of the rich and of officials, so Lydia was likely a woman of means, able to host Paul's whole party. Her name may be a nickname, "the Lydian woman." Thyatira later received one of the seven letters in Revelation, to "the angel of the church in Thyatira" (Revelation 2:18).

p: Lydia was a Gentile who honored Israel's God (on the God-fearers, see 10:2 and 13:16). She is the first named believer in Europe.
b: On the Gentile "God-fearers" or "God-worshipers" who joined the synagogues, and the inscription evidence for them, see the notes on 10:2, 13:16 and 13:43. What this verse adds is where Lydia met Israel's God: not in a synagogue, for Philippi seems to have had none, but at a gathering of women at a place of prayer by the river (16:13). She is one of the God-worshipers Luke names, along with Cornelius (10:2) and Titius Justus (18:7), and like them she was ready for Paul's message before he came. Luke gives the credit to God: "The Lord opened up her heart" (see the next note).

a: The Lord opened up her heart
p: Lydia listened, and the Lord opened her heart. Christians differ on how God's work and ours fit together.
b: The verb dianoigō, "open up," is the one Luke uses when the risen Jesus opened the Scriptures and the disciples' minds (Luke 24:32, 45) and when Paul opens the Scriptures in Thessalonica (17:3). Calvin took the verse as proof that faith is God's gift: hearing alone does nothing until God opens the heart. Wesleyan and Arminian readers agree that grace comes first, but hold that it enables a free response that can be refused. Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks of grace that goes before and works with human freedom. All agree that Luke credits the Lord, not Paul's skill, for Lydia's faith.

p: A Greek household included family members, slaves, freed servants and others who lived under its head.
b: Oikos, household, was the basic unit of ancient society: a head (here a woman, with no husband mentioned), relatives, slaves and dependents, who usually followed the religion of the head. Acts tells of several households coming to faith together: Cornelius (10:2, 44–48; 11:14), Lydia, the jailer (16:31–34) and Crispus (18:8); Paul baptized the household of Stephanas (1 Corinthians 1:16). Whether any of these included infants is one of the classic debates between churches (see the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter). Lydia's house then became the meeting place of the church at Philippi (16:40).

p: Python was the serpent of Delphi, Apollo's oracle. A slave girl with a "Python spirit" was thought to speak for the god.
b: Greek myth told that Apollo killed the serpent Python and took over the oracle at Delphi, where his priestess, the Pythia, gave answers in his name. By the first century "python" was also used for a person through whom a spirit spoke. Plutarch says that ventriloquists, once called engastrimythoi, "belly-talkers," were now called pythōnes (On the Obsolescence of Oracles 9, in the Moralia). The Septuagint uses engastrimythos for the medium at Endor, the woman "who has a ghost at her call" (1 Samuel 28:7). Luke does not treat the girl as a fraud: the spirit is real, it knows who Paul is, and it obeys the name of Jesus. Verdict: a real link of language to the Delphic cult, not a borrowing of the story.

a: slaves of the Most High God
t: "The Most High God" and "a way to be saved"
p: Both phrases sound different to a pagan ear. The spirit's words are true, yet open to misunderstanding.
b: "God Most High" is an old biblical title: Melchizedek "was a priest of God Most High" (Genesis 14:18). But Greeks also worshiped Zeus Hypsistos, "the Highest," and a hearer at Philippi could take the phrase for any top god. Demons in the Gospels use it too (Mark 5:7; Luke 8:28). The girl also says "a way to be saved," without "the": sōtēria could mean safety, health or rescue from many things. So the cry sounds like praise, yet it could make Paul look like one more preacher of one more god. Like Jesus, who did not let demons announce him (Luke 4:41), Paul would not take the spirit's advertising.
orig: δοῦλοι τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου (douloi tou theou tou hypsistou)

a: I order you, in the name of Jesus Christ, to come out of her!
p: Paul commands the spirit as Peter healed the lame man, in Jesus' name, and it leaves at once.
b: In Acts the name of Jesus carries his authority: Peter says "In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene" to the lame man (3:6), and the apostles heal and baptize in that name (2:38; 4:10). The contrast comes in Ephesus, where the sons of Sceva try to use "Jesus, the one Paul preaches" as a spell and are beaten by the spirit (19:13–16). The name is not a magic word; it works through those who belong to him. Luke says Paul was "thoroughly annoyed," a frank human touch, and he does not hide that the exorcism made trouble.

a: their hope of income had gone out with it
t: When the spirit went out, the money went out
p: Luke uses the same verb twice: the spirit "came out" and the owners' hope "went out."
b: Exēlthen, "it came out," ends 16:18; the next verse says the owners saw that their hope of income exēlthen, "had gone out." The play shows what the owners cared about: not the girl, but their ergasia, "business," the same word Luke uses for the silversmiths' trade in Ephesus, where the gospel again threatens the profits of religion (19:24–27). The girl herself drops out of the story. Luke does not say what became of her.

t: "They are Jews": the charge at Philippi
p: The owners turn a money complaint into a charge of spreading a foreign religion, playing on dislike of Jews.
b: The real grievance was lost income, but the charge is disturbing the peace and teaching customs Romans may not adopt. Roman tradition held that citizens should not take up foreign gods not approved by the state (Cicero, On the Laws 2.19, gives the old rule: "no one shall have gods of his own"). Judaism was tolerated, but making converts among Romans was frowned on, and around AD 49 Claudius expelled Jews from Rome (18:2). The irony is that the speakers cannot tell Jews and Christians apart, and Silas and Paul were in fact Roman citizens themselves (16:37).

p: The rod-bearers who attended Roman magistrates carried bundles of rods for public beatings.
b: The magistrates' attendants, the lictors (Greek rhabdouchoi, "rod-bearers," 16:35), carried the fasces, rods bound around an axe, the symbol of Roman power. A beating with them was severe and humiliating. Paul later counts three beatings with rods among his sufferings (2 Corinthians 11:25), and he reminds the Thessalonians how badly he had been treated at Philippi before he came to them (1 Thessalonians 2:2). Flogging a Roman citizen without trial was against Roman law (see 16:37).

t: The inner prison and the stocks
p: Roman prisons were dark and crowded. The inner cell, with feet locked in stocks, was the harshest place.
b: Prison in the Roman world was mostly for holding people until trial or punishment, not a sentence in itself. The inner part of a jail had no light or air, and stocks could spread a prisoner's legs painfully apart. Jeremiah suffered the same, put in the stocks by the priest Pashhur (Jeremiah 20:2). Brian Rapske's study of Paul in custody describes these conditions from ancient sources.

p: Beaten and locked in stocks, Paul and Silas pray and sing. Early Christians remembered the scene.
b: The verb hymneō means to sing praise, as Jesus and his disciples did after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30). The psalmist says, "In the middle of the night I rise to give you thanks" (Psalm 119:62). Tertullian, writing to Christians in prison around AD 200, said that the leg feels nothing in the stocks when the mind is in heaven (To the Martyrs 2). Luke adds that the prisoners "were listening in," a word for listening closely: the other prisoners are the first audience of this little sermon in song.

t: Prison doors that open by themselves
p: Greek stories told of gods freeing their followers from chains. Luke's story shares the motif but turns it around.
b: Acts has three prison escapes (5:19–20; 12:6–11; here). Greek readers knew a similar scene from Euripides' play The Bacchae, where the chains of the god Dionysus' followers fall off and the doors open by themselves (lines 443–448), and an earthquake shakes the king's palace. Some scholars think Luke used this kind of story on purpose; others think the motif was simply common. The difference is plain: Dionysus' followers escape, but Paul and Silas stay put, and the miracle ends with the jailer's rescue, not theirs. Verdict: a shared motif that Luke's readers would have recognized, used to make a different point.

a: ready to take his own life
p: A jailer who lost his prisoners could be punished with the penalty they faced. He chose death first.
b: Roman practice held guards responsible for escapes: Herod Agrippa had Peter's guards executed (12:19), and on the ship to Rome the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none would swim away (27:42). Facing disgrace and death, an ancient man might fall on his sword, as Saul did (1 Samuel 31:4). Paul's shout stops him, and the Bible's few stories of suicide are here answered by a rescue (see the topic page).

a: what do I have to do to be saved?
t: What did the jailer mean by "saved"?
p: He may have meant "safe" from the authorities or from the gods. Luke means more, and readers have argued how much the jailer knew.
b: Sōzō means to rescue or keep safe as well as to save from sin. Saved from danger: some think the frightened jailer only wanted to escape punishment or the anger of the god who shook the prison. Saved by God: others note he had probably heard the slave girl's cry for days, "They are telling you a way to be saved!" (16:17), and the prisoners' hymns. Either way, Paul and Silas answer with the full sense of the word, and Luke's readers hear the question every reader of Acts should ask (compare the crowd's question at Pentecost, 2:37).

p: Does the promise include a whole household because of one person's faith? Luke says they all heard the word.
b: The promise of salvation to a household (compare 11:14) reflects the ancient household, where members shared the head's religion. Covenant household: Reformed and Lutheran readers see a pattern of God's promise reaching a family through its head, as with Abraham's household (Genesis 17:7, 23). Each one believes: Baptist and other readers point out that the word was spoken "to everyone in his house" (16:32) and that the household rejoiced in faith (16:34), so each member heard and believed. Luke does not say whether there were small children. See the card on household baptism in this chapter.

p: The jailer washes Paul and Silas, then he is baptized. The scene pairs two washings in one night.
b: Elousen, "he washed," is the ordinary word for bathing; the next clause tells of baptism, a washing too (compare 22:16, where Ananias tells Saul to be baptized and have his sins washed away). The man who had laid stripes on them now cleans them, and is then cleaned himself. John Chrysostom drew out this pairing in his homilies on Acts. Baptism here comes "without delay," in the night, as with the Ethiopian official (8:36–38) and Saul (9:18): there is no long preparation in Acts, a fact churches that baptize after instruction have long discussed.

t: Roman citizens beaten without a trial
p: Roman law protected citizens from flogging without a trial. The magistrates had broken it.
b: The Porcian laws and later the Julian law on public violence forbade magistrates to beat a Roman citizen, let alone without a hearing. Cicero's speeches against Verres describe the outrage of a citizen flogged while crying, "I am a Roman citizen" (Against Verres 2.5.162). A citizen could carry a small certificate of his status, though false claims were punished severely. Why Paul and Silas did not speak up earlier is unclear: perhaps they did and were not heard in the uproar, or they chose to suffer and then used their rights to protect the young church. Paul uses his citizenship again in Jerusalem (22:25–29) and appeals to Caesar (25:11). How a Jew from Tarsus came to be a citizen, Luke says only that he was born one (22:28).

p: The church at Philippi met in Lydia's house. Paul's later letter shows women still leading there.
b: The first believers at Philippi Luke names were a businesswoman and her household and a jailer and his family. Of the slave girl he tells only that the spirit left her (16:18). They met in Lydia's home, the pattern of the house churches of the early mission (Romans 16:5; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 2). The church at Philippi stayed close to Paul: it sent him money more than once (Philippians 4:15–16), and his letter names two women, Euodia and Syntyche, who had worked hard beside him in the gospel (Philippians 4:2–3). About sixty years later Polycarp of Smyrna wrote to the same church (Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians).

a: They traveled the road through Amphipolis and Apollonia
p: Paul followed the Via Egnatia, the Roman highway across Macedonia, about a hundred miles to Thessalonica.
b: The Via Egnatia, built in the 140s BC, ran from the Adriatic coast across Macedonia to the Hellespont, passing through Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia and Thessalonica. Luke names only overnight stops, probably a day's travel apart for a mounted party, and says nothing about preaching there. Thessalonica (modern Thessaloniki) was the capital of the province of Macedonia, a large port and a free city with its own assembly and magistrates. It had a Jewish community large enough for a synagogue.

p: Paul's letters suggest a longer stay in Thessalonica. Most readers combine the two accounts.
b: Luke mentions three Sabbaths in the synagogue. But Paul's letter says he worked night and day so as not to be a burden (1 Thessalonians 2:9), and the Philippians sent him help in Thessalonica more than once (Philippians 4:16). The church Paul writes to is mostly made of people who turned from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9), not synagogue members. A longer stay: many think the three Sabbaths were only the synagogue phase, followed by weeks or months of work among Gentiles. Compression: others think Luke shortened the story to fit his pattern of synagogue, success, opposition and flight.

p: The verb is the one Luke uses for the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures to his disciples.
b: Dianoigō, "open up," links three scenes: on the Emmaus road the disciples' hearts burned while Jesus opened the Scriptures to them (Luke 24:32); Jesus opened their minds to understand them (Luke 24:45); and the Lord opened Lydia's heart (16:14). Paul here does what Jesus did, showing from Scripture that the Messiah "had to" suffer and rise. The word "laid out the evidence" (paratithēmi) means to set something before people, as a meal or an argument.

p: Most Jews of the time did not expect the Messiah to suffer and die. Paul had to argue it from Scripture.
b: Hopes for a Messiah in the first century were varied, but most pictured a royal deliverer who would defeat Israel's enemies (Psalms of Solomon 17). A crucified Messiah was, as Paul admits, a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). The early church found the suffering of the Messiah in passages like Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Psalm 16, which Acts quotes elsewhere (8:32–35; 2:25–31). Jewish tradition did later speak of a Messiah son of Joseph who would die in battle before the Messiah son of David came (Babylonian Talmud Sukkah 52a), but that idea is not clearly attested before the Talmud. Jewish readers today generally read Isaiah 53 of Israel as God's suffering servant.

p: The Greek verb comes from the word for a lot. They threw in their lot with Paul and Silas.
b: Proseklērōthēsan is found only here in the New Testament. It comes from klēros, "lot, share," the word used when Matthias was chosen by lot (1:26). It means to be assigned to a group, to join one's fortunes to someone's. Luke may mean that God allotted them to Paul; most take it as their own choice to join him. The converts are of three kinds: some Jews, many God-worshiping Greeks and a number of leading women, the pattern of Luke's story in the Greek cities.

p: Luke means the synagogue members who rejected Paul, not all Jews. The phrase was later used against Jews everywhere.
b: Some Jews in Thessalonica believed (17:4); "the Jews" here are those who did not, and the Byzantine text makes this explicit (see the variant). Their "jealousy" (zēloō) is also the word for zeal: they saw God-worshiping Gentiles, the synagogue's friends and patrons, leaving for a new movement, and saw a threat to the community's standing with the city. Paul had once shown the same zeal against the church (22:3–4; Galatians 1:13–14). Paul's own sharpest words about Jewish opponents come in a letter to this very church (1 Thessalonians 2:14–16). Such passages were later quoted to blame Jews as a people, a misuse Christian churches have since rejected (see the topic page).

p: Thessalonica was a free city with its own assembly, the dēmos. The mob wanted to bring Paul before it.
b: Dēmos, "the people," was the official assembly of citizens in a Greek city, the body behind the word "democracy." In 19:30–33 the same word is used of the crowd in the theater at Ephesus. Here the troublemakers hoped to haul Paul and Silas before a public meeting, but not finding them, they went to the officials instead (17:6).

p: Luke calls Thessalonica's officials politarchs, a title rare in literature but found in many inscriptions.
b: Greek literature hardly uses the word politarchēs, and older critics thought Luke had made a mistake. Then inscriptions turned up: some thirty or more, most from Macedonia and many from Thessalonica itself, including one on a Roman arch (the Vardar Gate, now in the British Museum) naming several politarchs. Colin Hemer lists this among many local details that Luke gets right: magistrates and lictors in the colony of Philippi (16:20, 35), politarchs here, the Areopagus at Athens, the proconsul of Achaia at Corinth (18:12). Such accuracy shows the author knew the Roman East well, though scholars still differ on what it proves about the rest of the story.

a: thrown the whole world into turmoil
p: The KJV's famous phrase. The Greek verb means to stir up revolt, a political charge.
b: Anastatoō means to unsettle, to stir up revolt: Claudius Lysias uses it of the Egyptian rebel (21:38), and Paul of the agitators in Galatia (Galatians 5:12). The KJV's "turned the world upside down" made it a compliment in English, but the accusers meant sedition across the empire (oikoumenē, the Roman world). The emperor Claudius, in a letter to the people of Alexandria in AD 41 (London Papyrus 1912), warned the Jews there against stirring up what he called a common plague for the whole world; the charge against Paul uses similar language of empire-wide unrest.
orig: οἱ τὴν οἰκουμένην ἀναστατώσαντες (hoi tēn oikoumenēn anastatōsantes)

a: They all break Caesar's decrees by saying that Jesus is another king.
p: The charge is treason. Some of the emperors' decrees banned predictions about rulers.
b: Calling Jesus "king" sounded like rebellion, the same charge brought against Jesus before Pilate (Luke 23:2; John 19:12). E. A. Judge has suggested that "Caesar's decrees" were the imperial bans on predicting a change of ruler, issued by Augustus in AD 11 and renewed by Tiberius, and that preaching a coming king and judgment sounded like such a prediction. Paul's letters to Thessalonica speak of the Lord's "coming" (parousia), a word also used for an emperor's visit (1 Thessalonians 4:15), and warn of people who say "Peace and security" (1 Thessalonians 5:3), close to Roman slogans. Luke's readers would see that the charge was false in its intent and true at its heart: Jesus is a king, but not one who takes up arms (compare John 18:36).
r: Luke 23:2; John 18:33–37; John 19:12; John 19:15; 1 Thessalonians 4:15; 1 Thessalonians 5:3; 16:4

p: The officials took security from Jason, likely a promise that the visitors would leave and cause no more trouble.
b: To hikanon, "what is sufficient," is a legal term for bail or security. Jason and the others had to guarantee the peace, probably by sending Paul away. William Ramsay suggested that this bond is what Paul meant when he wrote that he wanted to come back to Thessalonica again and again, but Satan stopped him (1 Thessalonians 2:18); it is an attractive guess but cannot be proved. Jason may be the Jason who later sends greetings with Paul from Corinth (Romans 16:21).

p: The Bereans welcomed the message and checked it against Scripture. Churches have drawn different lessons from them.
b: Eugenesteroi literally means "better-born"; here it means more noble-minded, more open and fair. The Bereans are praised for two things together: eagerness to hear and daily study of the Scriptures to see whether Paul was right. Scripture as the test: Protestant readers often cite them for testing all teaching by the Bible; many Bible-study groups are named "Berean" after them. Scripture and the living word: Catholic and Orthodox readers note that the Bereans received the apostles' spoken teaching and used their Scriptures, the Old Testament, to confirm it. Jewish readers may note that Luke's model believers here are synagogue Jews, doing what Jews had long done with the Scriptures.

p: The verb is the one used for the earthquake at Philippi. The opponents shake the city as the quake shook the prison.
b: Saleuō, "shake," described the earthquake that rocked the prison at Philippi (16:26) and the place where the believers prayed (4:31). Here the opponents from Thessalonica travel some fifty miles to Berea to "shake" the crowds there. The parallel may be accidental, but Luke likes such echoes: God shakes the prison open, and people shake a city shut.

a: Silas and Timothy should join him
p: Acts has them meet Paul again only at Corinth. Paul's letter says Timothy was sent back from Athens.
b: In Acts, Silas and Timothy stay in Berea (17:14) and rejoin Paul in Corinth (18:5). In 1 Thessalonians 3:1–2, Paul writes that he decided to stay alone at Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen the Thessalonians. Harmonized: many readers think Timothy (and perhaps Silas) did come to Athens as asked, and Paul sent them back to Macedonia, after which they all met again at Corinth. Simplified: others think Luke left out these comings and goings. The letter's "we" in 1 Thessalonians 3:1 may include Silas.

p: Athens was crowded with statues, altars and temples. Paul's spirit was "stirred to anger" at the sight.
b: Kateidōlos, found nowhere before this, means thick with idols. Ancient visitors agreed: Pausanias' guide to Greece (about AD 150) lists statue after statue, and the streets were lined with herms, pillars topped with the head of Hermes. The Acropolis held the Parthenon with Athena's great gold and ivory statue. Paul's reaction, paroxynō, "to provoke, anger," is the verb of 15:39 and the one the Greek Old Testament uses for God provoked by Israel's idols, as Moses grieved over "provoking him to anger" (Deuteronomy 9:18). Yet Paul's speech will begin with courtesy, not rage.

p: The two leading schools of the day. Paul's speech answers both: against the Epicureans' distant gods and the Stoics' god in everything.
b: Epicureans, followers of Epicurus (died 270 BC), taught that the gods, if they exist, live far away and take no interest in humans; the soul dies with the body; the goal of life is calm freedom from fear and pain. Stoics, from Zeno, who taught in the Stoa (porch) in the Athenian marketplace, taught that a divine reason (logos) runs through the universe, that all people are kin, and that one should live in agreement with nature. Paul's speech uses Stoic themes (God gives life to all, humans are his offspring) while rejecting the Epicurean idea of a distant god, and then breaks with both by announcing a judgment day and a resurrection.

p: Slang for a bird pecking up seeds, and so for a scrap-collector of other people's ideas.
b: Spermologos means "seed-gatherer," a word for rooks and crows pecking at grain, and then for a loafer who picks up scraps in the market, and a show-off who repeats half-learned ideas. Demosthenes threw the word at his rival Aeschines (On the Crown 127). Most English versions say "babbler," which loses the picture. The philosophers dismiss Paul as an amateur who has picked up bits of philosophy without understanding them.

a: the good news of Jesus and the resurrection
p: Some hearers may have thought Paul was announcing two new gods, Jesus and a goddess called "Resurrection."
b: The plural "foreign deities" has puzzled readers, since Paul preached one God. John Chrysostom suggested that the Athenians took Anastasis, "Resurrection," for the name of a goddess, a female partner to Jesus; Athenians did worship abstract powers such as Peace and Mercy. Many modern scholars find this likely; others think the plural is just a sneer. "Announcing foreign deities" also recalls the charge against Socrates, condemned in Athens for bringing in new divinities (Plato, Apology 24b; Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.1.1). Luke presents Paul, like Socrates, debating daily in the marketplace with whoever came by.

p: Areopagus means "Ares' Hill," and it was also the name of Athens' oldest council. Paul may have stood before the council.
b: The Areopagus is a rocky hill below the Acropolis, named for Ares, the god of war (Latin Mars, hence the KJV's "Mars' hill" in 17:22). The ancient council that met there kept the name, and in Roman times it had authority over religious matters and education, and probably met in the Royal Stoa in the marketplace. A formal hearing: many scholars think Paul was brought before the council to explain his teaching, perhaps to see if he could lecture in the city, though not on trial for his life. An informal gathering: others think he was simply taken to the hill to speak in a quieter place. The convert "Dionysius the Areopagite" (17:34) was a member of the council.

p: Ancient writers mocked the Athenians' craving for news. Luke adds his own wry comment.
b: The Greek kainoteron, "newer," means the very latest thing. Athenians had long been teased for this. The orator Demosthenes rebuked them for going about the marketplace asking whether there was anything new (First Philippic 10), and Thucydides has the politician Cleon tell them they are slaves to every novelty (3.38). Luke's aside is both a joke and a setup: Paul brings something truly new, the resurrection, and they do not want it.

p: The Greek can be praise or blame. The KJV says "too superstitious." Most think Paul meant a polite opening.
b: Deisidaimonesterous comes from deisidaimōn, "fearing the divine powers." It could mean pious or devout, or, in philosophical writers such as Theophrastus and Plutarch, superstitious and fearful. The KJV took the second sense: "ye are too superstitious." Most modern interpreters think Paul begins politely, as speakers did, while choosing a word with a double edge his hearers would catch. Festus uses the related noun neutrally of the Jewish "religion" (25:19).

p: Ancient writers mention altars at Athens to "unknown gods." No altar with the singular wording has been found.
b: Pausanias, describing the road from the harbor at Phaleron to Athens, mentions altars "of gods called unknown" (Description of Greece 1.1.4), and Philostratus says that at Athens altars are set up even to unknown divinities (Life of Apollonius 6.3). Diogenes Laertius tells how, during a plague, the Cretan wise man Epimenides had sheep released and altars built wherever they lay down, to whatever god was concerned, so that nameless altars could still be seen (Lives of the Philosophers 1.110). Jerome claimed the inscription really read in the plural, "to the gods of Asia, Europe and Africa, to unknown and foreign gods" (Commentary on Titus 1:12), and thought Paul adapted it. A singular altar is not attested, but it is quite possible among the many.

a: He does not dwell in shrines that hands have made.
p: Paul says what Stephen said and what Solomon admitted: no building can hold God.
b: Solomon, dedicating the Temple, asked, "But can God truly make his home on earth?" (1 Kings 8:27), and Isaiah heard the LORD say, "The heavens are my throne, / and the earth is the stool for my feet" (Isaiah 66:1). Stephen quoted that verse when he said the Most High does not live in handmade houses (7:48–50). Spoken within sight of the Parthenon, the line is bold, but Greek philosophers would agree: Zeno the Stoic taught that temples should not be built for the gods, as Plutarch reports. Paul begins on common ground with the Stoics and with Israel's Scriptures at once.

a: Nor do human hands tend to him
p: God is not a statue waiting for servants to feed and dress it. He is the giver of life and breath.
b: Therapeuō was the word for the care temple servants gave to a god's image: washing, dressing, offering food. Paul says God needs no such service. The psalmist has God say, "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you, / for the world and everything in it is mine" (Psalm 50:12). Isaiah calls him the one who "gives the people on it breath" (Isaiah 42:5). Greek philosophers also taught that the divine lacks nothing, so Paul's hearers could agree. The twist comes later: the God who needs nothing calls everyone to account (17:30–31).

a: every nation of humankind out of one person
p: The whole human race comes from one ancestor. Athenians, who boasted that they sprang from their own soil, heard a challenge.
b: Paul means Adam (Genesis 1:27; 2:7), though he does not name him. Athenians prided themselves on being autochthonous, born from the soil of Attica itself and not immigrants like other Greeks (Plato's Menexenus praises them for it). Paul says every nation comes from one origin. The verse has had a double history. In America it was quoted by abolitionists and by the civil rights movement against racism, often in the KJV form "of one blood" (see the variant). Some defenders of segregation used its second half, the "limits of the places where they would live," to argue for separating races, a reading most interpreters reject: the verse is about God's care for every nation, not about keeping them apart.
r: Genesis 1:27–28; Genesis 10:32; Genesis 11:8–9; Deuteronomy 32:8; Malachi 2:10; Romans 5:12

a: their set seasons and the limits of the places where they would live
p: Paul may mean the seasons of the year and the zones where people can live, or the eras and borders of nations.
b: Nature: many, following Martin Dibelius, read this as the language of natural theology: God fixed the seasons of the year and the habitable zones of the earth, signs of his care, as in Paul's speech at Lystra, where God gives rain from heaven and seasons of harvest (14:17). History: others read the times and limits as the eras and borders of nations, as in Daniel 2:21 or the Song of Moses: "he marked out the peoples' borders" (Deuteronomy 32:8). Both readings make the same point: God arranged the world so that people would look for him (17:27).

p: The verb means feeling around in the dark, like a blind man. People search for God, but not with clear sight.
b: Psēlaphaō means to touch or feel about. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the blind feeling their way: "You will feel your way at noon the way a blind person feels his way in the dark" (Deuteronomy 28:29), and "We grope at the wall like blind men" (Isaiah 59:10). In Homer the blinded Cyclops gropes for the men escaping from his cave (Odyssey 9.416). Paul's picture is hopeful and sober at once: people can seek and even find, yet without revelation they are in the dark. That is why he goes on to call the past "times of not knowing" (17:30).
r: Deuteronomy 4:29; Deuteronomy 28:29; Isaiah 55:6; Isaiah 59:10; Jeremiah 29:13; Romans 1:19–21

a: in him we live and move and exist
p: Perhaps a line from the Cretan poet Epimenides, but the evidence is late. Many think Paul is using a common Stoic idea.
b: The SBL and most editions do not mark this line as a quotation. A ninth-century Syriac commentary by Ishodad of Merv preserves a poem attributed to Epimenides of Crete, in which Minos addresses Zeus: the Cretans who built his tomb are liars (compare Titus 1:12), "for you live and abide for ever; in you we live and move and have our being." On this basis some scholars think Paul quotes Epimenides here, but the attribution is late and uncertain. Others think the triad of living, moving and being is Paul's own summary of Stoic belief in a God in whom all things exist. Either way, Paul borrows his hearers' language to describe the God of Israel. ("Have our being" is the KJV's English; the Plain English Translation says "exist.")

p: A line from the poet Aratus of Cilicia, originally about Zeus. A Jewish writer had already applied it to God.
b: Aratus, a Stoic poet from Soli in Cilicia, not far from Paul's Tarsus, began his poem Phaenomena (about 275 BC) with Zeus, "for we are also his offspring" (line 5). The Stoic Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus has a similar line. Over a century before Paul, the Jewish teacher Aristobulus quoted Aratus' opening lines, putting "God" where the poet had "Zeus" (quoted in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 13.12). Paul says "some of your poets": the idea was common property. He does not endorse Zeus; he takes the poet's truth, that humans are God's kin, and draws a Jewish conclusion from it: then God cannot be a statue (17:29).

p: Paul uses the philosophers' abstract word for divinity, then makes the prophets' point against idols.
b: To theion, "the divine," was a common term in Greek philosophy for the divine nature, without naming a particular god. Paul speaks his hearers' language. His argument is Israel's: if humans, living beings, are God's offspring, God cannot resemble gold, silver or stone carved by human skill. Isaiah asks, "So who will you say God is like?" (Isaiah 40:18), and mocks the craftsman who makes an idol from the same wood he burns (Isaiah 44:9–20). Jews had long made this case to Greeks, as in the Wisdom of Solomon (13–15).
r: Isaiah 40:18–20; Isaiah 44:9–20; Isaiah 46:5–7; Psalm 115:4–8; Exodus 20:4; Romans 1:22–23; Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–19

a: God has looked past those times of not knowing
p: God overlooked past ignorance. Readers ask what that means for people who never heard the gospel.
b: Hyperidōn means "having overlooked": not approving, but not yet judging. Paul said something similar at Lystra: in past generations God let the nations go their own ways (14:16; compare Romans 3:25, God's passing over sins). A time of grace now ending: most read the verse as saying that God's patience has given way to a clear command to repent, now that the resurrection has made his will known. Hope for the unevangelized: some, including many Catholic and some Protestant theologians, have drawn from it the hope that God judges people by the light they had (compare Lumen Gentium 16). Others reply that the verse speaks of God's patience, not of salvation without the gospel.

a: judge the world in the right way
t: The day of judgment and the appointed man
p: Paul uses the Psalms' promise that God will judge the world rightly, and names a man as the judge.
b: "He will judge the world in the right way" comes from the Psalms (Psalm 9:8; Psalm 96:13; Psalm 98:9), where the LORD is coming to judge. Paul says God will do this "through a man he has marked out," as Peter told Cornelius that Jesus is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead (10:42). The thought recalls Daniel's "one like a son of man" given rule (Daniel 7:13–14). Paul does not name Jesus here, though his hearers knew whom he preached (17:18). The proof is the resurrection: pistis, usually "faith," here means a guarantee or ground for faith. "In the right way" renders en dikaiosynē, usually "in righteousness" on this site; the Plain English Translation uses the Psalms' wording here so the allusion can be heard.
r: Psalm 9:8; Psalm 96:13; Psalm 98:9; 10:42; Daniel 7:13–14; John 5:22–27; Romans 2:16; 2 Corinthians 5:10

p: Greeks could accept an immortal soul, but a raised body seemed absurd. Athens' own drama said so.
b: Many Greeks believed the soul lived on after death; few could imagine the body raised. In Aeschylus' tragedy The Eumenides, set at the founding of the Areopagus court, the god Apollo says that when the dust has soaked up a man's blood, once he is dead, there is no rising again (anastasis; lines 647–648). Paul's word is the same. The church Paul founded at Corinth soon after had the same doubt a few years later (1 Corinthians 15:12). Luke does not call the speech a failure: some mocked, some wanted more, and some believed (17:34).

a: And so Paul left their company.
p: Some say Paul's speech failed and taught him to preach only the cross at Corinth. Others disagree.
b: A lesson learned: William Ramsay and others argued that Paul, disappointed at Athens, resolved at Corinth "to know nothing" among them except Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:1–2). No failure: most recent commentators answer that Luke presents the speech as a model, ending with Jesus and the resurrection, that some believed, and that 1 Corinthians 2 is about Corinth's love of rhetoric, not a regret about Athens. Luke's composition: critical scholars such as Dibelius regarded the speech as Luke's own model sermon to educated Gentiles, not a record of Paul's words; others (Bruce, Witherington) think it summarizes what Paul could well have said.

p: A member of the Areopagus council and a woman named Damaris believed. Later legends grew around Dionysius.
b: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council, a man of rank. Bishop Dionysius of Corinth, about AD 170, said he became the first bishop of Athens (reported by Eusebius, Church History 4.23.3). Around AD 500 an unknown Christian writer, steeped in Neoplatonism, wrote influential works under his name, the Pseudo-Dionysius, which shaped medieval mysticism. In France he was later merged with Saint Denis, first bishop of Paris. Of Damaris nothing more is known; John Chrysostom guessed she was Dionysius' wife (On the Priesthood 4.7). That Luke names a woman among the few converts at Athens fits his habit of noting women of standing (17:4, 12). The Western text leaves her out (see the variant).
